title: NBA Team Winning Percentage and Field-Goal Percentage
text:
The question
Which factors most influence an NBA team’s winning percentage? For this project we will seek to predict win percentage for NBA teams given stats such as season total rebounds, shot percentage, free-throw percentage, assists, blocks, etc. The intended audience for this project is Dr. White, as well as any NBA fans in our class. Understanding factors that contribute to win percentage is important for die-hard fans to contextualize their team’s performance over the course of a season. The answer also matters for sports broadcasters so that they can help their viewers understand why certain teams are better than others.
The dataset used in this study is the NBA Teams Stat 2000–2023 dataset, created by bluedreamv1b3 and hosted on Kaggle: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/bluedreamv1b3/nba-teams-stat-2000-2023. The specific file analyzed is pergame_stats_total.csv. The observational unit is an NBA team season (a single NBA franchise’s regular season performance in a given year, e.g., 2015-16 Golden State Warriors). The dataset contains 720 observations (30 teams across 24 seasons from 2000 to 2023) and approximately 25 to 30 feature columns. Response Variable: Win-Loss Percentage (W/L% or calculated as \(\text{Wins} / (\text{Wins} + \text{Losses})\)).Candidate Predictors: Per-game team statistics, including Points Per Game (PTS), Field Goal Percentage (FG%), Three-Point Percentage (3P%), Rebounds (TRB), Assists (AST), Steals (STL), Blocks (BLK), Turnovers (TOV), and Opponent Points Allowed (OPTS or PTSd). The data was collected via web scraping from public statistical archives on Basketball-Reference.com. Because Basketball-Reference makes aggregate sports statistics publicly available for fan and research use, retrieving and sharing this dataset for academic/educational non-commercial purposes carries no privacy concerns (it contains aggregate team performance metrics, no private personal data). Team win/loss percentage in professional basketball is directly driven by offensive efficiency (scoring capacity) and defensive efficiency (preventing opponent scores). Because pergame_stats_total.csv contains box-score metrics capturing both offensive productivity and turnover/rebounding controls, it provides sufficient empirical information to model and predict team win percentage.

# Load required packages
library(tidyverse)

# Read per-game stats and advanced stats datasets
pergame_data <- read_csv("nba_data_2000_2023/pergame_stats_total.csv")
adv_data <- read_csv("nba_data_2000_2023/advanced_stats_total.csv")

# Clean team names by removing playoff asterisks (*) and filtering out header rows
pergame_clean <- pergame_data %>%
  mutate(
    Team_clean = str_replace_all(Team, "\\*", ""),
    Team_clean = str_trim(Team_clean)
  )

adv_clean <- adv_data %>%
  filter(Team != "Team") %>%
  mutate(
    Team_clean = str_replace_all(Team, "\\*", ""),
    Team_clean = str_trim(Team_clean),
    W = as.numeric(W),
    L = as.numeric(L),
    Year = as.numeric(Year),
    WL_percent = W / (W + L)
  )

# Merge the datasets by Team and Year
nba_full <- pergame_clean %>%
  inner_join(adv_clean, by = c("Team_clean", "Year"))

# Check dimensions and variables of the merged dataset
glimpse(nba_full)

library(ggplot2)

# Create scatter plot of Points Per Game vs Regular Season Win/Loss Percentage colored by Field Goal %
ggplot(nba_full, aes(x = PTS, y = WL_percent, color = FG_Percent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "blue", high = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "NBA Team Points Per Game vs. Win-Loss Percentage (2000–2023)",
    subtitle = "Higher scoring teams generally achieve higher winning percentages",
    x = "Points Per Game (PTS)",
    y = "Win-Loss Percentage (W/L%)",
    color = "Field Goal %"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )









The scatter plot displays a positive linear trend between a team’s points per game (PTS) and its win-loss percentage (WL_percent), indicating that higher-scoring teams generally achieve higher winning records. Additionally, teams with higher field goal percentages (represented by brighter red markers) tend to cluster toward the right side of the distribution with elevated scoring outputs and win percentages. However, because this is an observational study of seasonal team statistics, we cannot conclude that increasing scoring directly causes more wins without accounting for defensive performance, opponent points allowed, and other confounding variables.


Show code
baseline_dir <- if (dir.exists("nba_data_2000_2023")) {
  "nba_data_2000_2023"
} else {
  "Data Set/archive Data Set"
}
baseline_pergame <- read_csv(
  file.path(baseline_dir, "pergame_stats_total.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE)
baseline_advanced <- read_csv(
  file.path(baseline_dir, "advanced_stats_total.csv"),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), show_col_types = FALSE)

baseline_shooting <- baseline_pergame %>%
  filter(Team != "League Average") %>%
  transmute(Team_clean = str_trim(str_remove_all(Team, fixed("*"))),
            Year = as.integer(Year), FG_pct = 100 * FG_Percent)
baseline_records <- baseline_advanced %>%
  transmute(Team_clean = str_trim(str_remove_all(Team, fixed("*"))),
            Year = suppressWarnings(as.integer(Year)),
            wins = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(W)),
            losses = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(L))) %>%
  filter(!is.na(wins), !is.na(losses), wins + losses > 0)

stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(baseline_shooting[c("Team_clean", "Year")]),
          !anyDuplicated(baseline_records[c("Team_clean", "Year")]),
          nrow(anti_join(baseline_shooting, baseline_records,
                        by = c("Team_clean", "Year"))) == 0,
          nrow(anti_join(baseline_records, baseline_shooting,
                        by = c("Team_clean", "Year"))) == 0)
baseline_data <- inner_join(
  baseline_shooting, baseline_records, by = c("Team_clean", "Year"),
  relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
  mutate(win_pct = 100 * wins / (wins + losses))
stopifnot(all(complete.cases(baseline_data[c("FG_pct", "win_pct")])) )

baseline_model <- lm(win_pct ~ FG_pct, data = baseline_data)
baseline_ci <- confint(baseline_model)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(Term = c("Intercept", "Field-goal percentage"),
             Estimate = unname(coef(baseline_model)),
             Lower_95 = baseline_ci[, 1], Upper_95 = baseline_ci[, 2]),
  digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Baseline coefficients and conventional 95% confidence intervals")

We use simple linear regression to predict regular-season winning percentage from field-goal percentage. This provides an interpretable starting point for examining whether team-seasons with better shooting tend to have higher winning percentages. Both variables are expressed on a 0–100 scale.
Across 715 team-seasons, a one-percentage-point higher field-goal percentage (for example, 46% instead of 45%) is associated with an estimated 5.1 percentage points higher winning percentage. The conventional 95% confidence interval is 4.54 to 5.65 percentage points. The model explains approximately 31.4% of the observed variation in winning percentage. This is an association using same-season statistics, not a causal effect or evidence of accurate preseason forecasting.
A specific limitation is that shooting percentage alone omits defensive performance: teams with similar shooting percentages can allow different numbers of points. Adding defensive rating could help explain these differences. The confidence interval assumes independent errors with constant variance; repeated franchises and shared seasons may violate those assumptions, so the uncertainty is preliminary. Linear regression can also produce predictions outside the 0–100 range.
